title: US Parasite Outbreak Linked to Mexican Lettuce Surges Past 10,000 Cases
excerpt: A cyclosporiasis outbreak traced to shredded iceberg lettuce from a Guanajuato supplier has sickened thousands across 41 states, triggering recalls, travel alerts, and a diplomatic spat between Washington and Mexico City.
body:
• The US is experiencing the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak in history, surpassing 10,000 suspected cases and 4,173 confirmed infections across 41 states.
  • Michigan has reported over 7,171 cases, making it the state with the highest number of infections.
  • The outbreak has been linked to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, prompting a nationwide recall and removal from Taco Bell's supply chain.
  • 308 people have been hospitalized due to the outbreak, but no deaths have been reported.

The largest cyclosporiasis outbreak in US history has blown past 10,000 suspected cases, with the CDC reporting 4,173 laboratory-confirmed infections across 41 states as of July 21 and at least 7,400 additional cases awaiting confirmation. Michigan alone accounts for over 7,171 cases, according to state health officials on July 22. Nationally, 308 people have been hospitalized. No deaths have been reported.

The intestinal infection, caused by the microscopic parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis, is spread through contaminated food or water and produces severe diarrhea, cramping, nausea, and fatigue. Symptoms can take up to two weeks to appear after exposure, complicating efforts to trace the source.

The Lettuce Trail to Mexico

The FDA's investigation has converged on a single supplier: Taylor Farms de Mexico, based in the central Mexican state of Guanajuato. The agency linked shredded iceberg lettuce from the supplier to a five-state outbreak cluster among Taco Bell patrons in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia.

https://x.com/telesurenglish/status/2079683426605830218

On July 17, Taylor Farms issued a voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico. Taco Bell removed Taylor Farms lettuce from its nationwide supply chain, and Walmart pulled Marketside Bagged Iceberg Salad products distributed by the company across 27 states.

A separate FDA border test initially came back positive for cyclospora on July 18, but was later reclassified as a false positive on July 19. The FDA clarified on X that the false-positive result "DOES NOT change the basis for FDA's ongoing outbreak investigation or the overwhelming epidemiological data supporting the current voluntary recall by Taylor Farms."

"The short shelf life of fresh produce means that by the time an outbreak is traced to a supplier, it may have already been consumed—adding to the difficulty in testing."

— Thomas Lew, Assistant Clinical Professor of Medicine, Stanford University School of Medicine

Mexico Pushes Back, Kennedy Says Outbreak 'Under Control'

Mexico's Health Minister David Kershenobich rejected the FDA's findings on July 21. "So far, no evidence has been found to indicate that it originated there," he said at a press conference, according to Reuters. "However, we are taking all precautions in case that were the case."

Mexico's sanitary regulator Cofepris and agricultural safety body Senasica have launched an interagency investigation, conducting what they described as "strictly preventive" inspections and traceability analyses at the implicated farms.

On the American side, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. declared the outbreak "under control" in a July 21 briefing, pushing back against criticism that Trump administration cuts to the CDC's FoodNet surveillance program had weakened the government's ability to track foodborne illness. "We did cuts in the FoodNet program, but they were for redundant surveillance," Kennedy said.

Food safety attorney Bill Marler, who has handled cyclospora cases for 33 years, told USA TODAY that testing difficulties are inherent to the parasite. "By the time you figure out the outbreak is going on, the product is long gone. That's especially true for perishable products," he said. Taylor Farms' Guanajuato facilities were previously linked to a 2013 cyclosporiasis outbreak that sickened more than 600 people in 25 states.

Travel Alerts and the Diaspora Angle

The CDC has logged 767 travel-linked cyclosporiasis cases since May 1, involving food or water consumed outside the United States. Canada updated its US travel advisory on July 17, flagging the outbreak for travelers heading south of the border.

For Indian Americans, the outbreak carries a double edge. Cyclospora is endemic in South and Southeast Asia, including India, where cases tend to spike before the monsoon season. Diaspora members familiar with the parasite from the subcontinent may not expect exposure through American fast-food chains or bagged salads at Walmart. Those planning summer trips to Mexico—one of the most popular international destinations for US travelers—should take extra precautions with raw produce and unfiltered water, the CDC advises.

The agency recommends thoroughly washing all fruits and vegetables under running water and cooking produce to at least 158°F (70°C) to kill the oocysts. Avoiding recalled lettuce products and monitoring the FDA's updated recall list remain the most direct preventive steps.

What Comes Next

The CDC expects case counts to keep climbing, citing a six-week reporting lag between illness onset and official tallying. Former FDA Commissioner Scott Gottlieb noted that Taco Bell accounts for only about 60% of the multistate outbreak cases, meaning other supply chains may also be involved. The FDA said additional brands, restaurants, and retailers could be implicated as the investigation widens.

For now, Taco Bell CEO Sean Tresvant's LinkedIn message to customers summarized the stakes: "We aren't entitled to your loyalty. We earn it one meal at a time."
